name: Gold colloid

lead: Gold colloid, or colloidal gold, is a suspension of gold nanoparticles in a liquid, usually water. It is marketed as a premium ingredient in some skincare and cosmetic products, where it is associated with a glowing, luxurious finish.
Much of the published research concerns gold nanoparticles in medicine, such as imaging, diagnostics and cancer therapy, rather than skin appearance.

paras: People encounter it as an ingredient in serums, masks and creams, applied like any other topical product. It is generally one component of a product rather than a stand-alone routine.
Reviews describe gold nanoparticles as generally biocompatible, but toxicity depends on particle size and the chemicals coating them. Cosmetic products can still cause individual skin reactions.

angle.text: Brands use gold colloid as a prestige ingredient, and users apply products containing it hoping for a brighter, smoother-looking complexion.

lead: Colloidal gold is a suspension of gold nanoparticles in a fluid, usually water. Small spherical particles look wine red, while larger ones or nanorods appear blue-purple.[1]

Gold has long carried a premium association. Medieval writers described 'soluble gold' as a cure for various diseases, and Michael Faraday prepared the first pure sample in 1857.[1] In skincare, gold appears as a luxury ingredient in some products.

Published research on colloidal gold concentrates on medicine and laboratory work: reviews describe gold nanoparticles as candidates for drug delivery, imaging and photothermal cancer therapy.[2][3] Trials of colloidal gold on skin appearance were not found.
infobox: Wine red to blue-purple by particle size

paras: Colloidal gold colour comes from surface plasmon resonance of gold particles under 100 nm.[1]

Gold stained glass in ancient times, and the 4th-century Lycurgus Cup changes colour with light.[1] Francis Anthony wrote about soluble gold in 1618, Faraday produced the first pure sample in 1857, and Richard Zsigmondy made dilute colloidal gold in 1898.[1]

Gold nanoparticles are reported to be generally biocompatible, though toxic concentrations are not fully defined. Toxicity appears to depend more on capping ligands than gold itself, and particle size matters: 1.4 nm particles were more toxic in cell studies than 15 nm ones.[1]
No studies found for cosmetic skin use. Separate research, mostly laboratory and review work, has examined gold nanoparticles in cancer treatment and imaging.[2][3]
